voiceover.text: So, who actually runs health in Australia? Someone leaves hospital on a Friday afternoon with three new medicines, a wound that needs dressing, and no car. List everyone who'd need to do something next week to make that work. Then count how many of them work for the same organisation. That second list is very short.

scenes.title: who pays, who delivers, who sets the rules

voiceover.text: Ask three questions of any service. Who pays for it, who delivers it, and who sets its rules? They're often three different bodies. The federal government is mainly a funder and regulator. It pays for doctors' visits through Medicare, subsidises medicines, funds aged care and disability support, pays a large share of public hospital costs, and regulates medicines and insurance. State and territory governments run the public hospitals and ambulances, plus community and mental health services, and outbreak response. Local government, your council, inspects food premises, runs some immunisation clinics, and builds footpaths, parks and sports grounds, which is health policy even if nobody calls it that. Why split it this way? An entitlement that must be the same everywhere needs one national payer. Hospitals need daily local management. So trace a GP visit. Medicare pays, and a private practice delivers it.

Outside government is the non-government sector, and it has two parts. Private for-profit providers deliver most GP and specialist care, private hospitals, pharmacy and health insurance. Not-for-profit organisations put any surplus back into their purpose. They deliver much of aged care, community care and disability services, community-controlled health services, and health charities. You met them as advocates in Year 11. Here's what they do that government can't. They earn trust where government reaches people badly, they advocate and hold government to account, they fund research and peer support, and they test new ideas small. Their limits matter too. Contracts are often short, they sit where they happen to be, not where need is, and profit doesn't always line up with health, so government regulates them. So public and private are far less separate than they look.

Draw a line from each funder to each service it pays for, and the lines cross. Every crossing is a seam, a boundary where responsibility blurs and a person can fall through. It has benefits. Decisions sit closer to people, and states can adapt to local needs. But it creates four predictable problems. Cost-shifting: when two funders each pay part of someone's care, each gains if the other pays more. Gaps at the boundary: a patient is ready to leave hospital, but no aged care place is funded, so they wait in a hospital bed. Duplication: different rules, forms and records for the same person. And accountability that's hard to find, because when care goes wrong, nobody owns all of it. They hit hardest on people who need several services at once: older people, people with disability, and people with several chronic conditions.

scenes.title: person-centred care, and the carry test

voiceover.text: That's why this dotpoint pairs with person-centred care. It isn't politeness, and it isn't patient satisfaction. It means care is organised around the person's goals and circumstances, not around what suits the providers. You can check it five ways. The person's goals set the plan. Decisions are shared, with options and risks explained before choosing. There's one plan everyone can see, including the person. There's a known contact who knows the history. And housing, income, carers, culture and language count as part of the care. Then one quick test. Does the person have to carry information between services? If they do, the system has handed its coordination job to the patient.

They work together at three levels, and each fails differently. Around the person: a team that shares one care plan, discharge planning that starts on admission, a care coordinator, and shared records. Between organisations: regional bodies that buy in services to fill local gaps, referral agreements between hospitals and community providers, and government contracting not-for-profits to deliver care. At the system level: funding agreements between governments, national standards, and shared data. It works when someone is accountable for the whole person, information moves without them, and funding follows the person. It fails when it sits on top of funding that still pulls providers apart, or rests on goodwill and short contracts.
Two things to remember. The payer is often not the provider, so the lines cross. And ask, does the person carry the information?

Two exam questions. First. Service one: aged care services in an older person's home, delivered by a not-for-profit organisation. Service two: an officer inspecting the food handling in a local café. For each, name who funds it and who delivers it, and say whether it sits at a seam with another part of the system. Pause here to answer.

Home aged care is mostly federally funded, and a not-for-profit delivers it. That split alone isn't a seam. The seam is where it meets the state-run hospital, where discharge delays happen. The council funds and delivers the café inspection, under state law, so there's hardly a seam. The classic mistake is thinking not-for-profit means privately paid for.

Second. A woman with diabetes and heart failure sees a GP, a hospital heart clinic and a not-for-profit nursing service. Each keeps its own records, and she brings a handwritten medicine list to every visit. Explain why her care isn't person-centred, and outline one collaboration that would fix it. Pause here to answer.

She's carrying the information between three services, so the system has handed her its coordination job. There's no single plan, and no one owns the whole picture. One fix: a shared care plan and a shared record across all three, with her GP as the known contact. The classic mistake is saying the staff should be kinder. Person-centred is about structure, not manners.

So ask who pays, who delivers and who sets the rules, find the seams, and test whether the person carries the information. Now look at the funders' side of the map. Every line is money. How much of it goes to treating illness, and how much to preventing it?
